Record version: 1.0. Prepared for the fictional decision cutoff 2026-11-23 15:00 UTC. Public references retrieved 2026-11-23; this record is attributed research context, not a customer contract, legal opinion, product assessment or certification.

S01: W3C's WCAG 2.2 Recommendation, published 12 December 2024, describes conformance for complete processes: where pages form a sequence needed to accomplish an activity, every page in that process must conform at the stated level. Its example concerns completing a purchase. This is a technical standard's scope rule, not evidence that the fictional service has been evaluated or that any particular law applies. Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG22-20241212/#conformance-reqs .

S02: W3C WAI's Easy Checks resource, updated 9 August 2023, says a quick review examines only some accessibility issues. Passing those checks can coexist with substantial barriers, so comprehensive assessment requires more extensive evaluation. The resource includes keyboard operation, focus, form labels and errors among its introductory checks. Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/preliminary/ .

S03: W3C WAI's interim-repair guidance, updated 12 August 2026, recommends considering key tasks and all their steps, frequently used or relevant content, and reported barriers when prioritizing repairs. It also recommends validating proposed changes early and involving disabled people when possible. It discusses phased work without establishing that an untested workaround resolves an individual barrier. Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/planning/interim-repairs/ .

S04: W3C WAI's accessibility-statement guidance, updated 11 March 2021, recommends telling users the applied standard, contact route, known limitations, testing environments and relevant prerequisites. It distinguishes a useful statement from a technical assessment or declaration of conformity and recommends ordinary language describing the actual limitation. Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/planning/statements/ .

S05: W3C WAI's user-evaluation guidance, with links updated 30 April 2024, says user involvement complements standards evaluation. A small study cannot establish accessibility for everyone with the same disability or for people with other disabilities. Reports should describe evaluation scope, methods and participants rather than generalize a limited result. Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/involving-users/ .

The remaining records concern LanternPath, a fictional application vendor, and the fictional Rivermere Skills Trust. No real institution, complainant, employee, disability record or customer transcript is represented. The scenario combines independently authored launch, support, procurement and operations facts. Public guidance supplies concepts about process scope and evidence limits; it does not supply fictional acceptance terms, signatory powers, contractual remedies or launch decisions. Those appear only in the dated business records.

All source paragraphs are brief original factual paraphrases. No webpage text, screenshots, transcript or licensed dataset is reproduced. Their local hashes identify the authored paragraphs, not the current or historical bytes of a webpage. Live pages can change after retrieval. The fictional cutoff is separate from publication and retrieval dates, and no later product outcome is available. A provider roadmap, small test, standards target and supplier declaration have different evidential roles. The dossier does not ask support to determine applicable law, certify conformance, diagnose a person's disability or make a universal claim about assistive technology.
# E02 — Order, rollout and decision roles

Record version: ORDER-31.2. Owner: Rivermere procurement coordinator Imani Hale. Signed order dated 2026-09-14; launch schedule confirmed 2026-11-18 10:00 UTC. Account annotation current 2026-11-23 11:00 UTC. All names and terms are synthetic.

Rivermere Skills Trust purchased a twelve-month LanternPath subscription for a training-grant application service. The order totals £36,000 excluding tax: £30,000 subscription and £6,000 implementation. The implementation amount is settled. The subscription invoice is scheduled for December 1, payable in thirty days; no automatic debit is configured. The service period starts December 1 even if public intake is deferred unless the parties execute a written variation. Support cannot say that stopping a launch stops the invoice, nor that an unpaid invoice has already been refunded. Procurement can request a variation but only Trust executive director Ada Fen and LanternPath commercial director Lena Orr can sign it.

Public applications are planned to open November 24 at 09:00 UTC and close December 4 at 17:00 UTC. All operational times in this record set use UTC. The Trust's board pack is due today at 17:00, with public notices scheduled at 18:00. The program has 120 training places and expects roughly 600 applications. The deadline is administrative, not asserted here as a legal requirement. Ada may change it after checking funder communications. An extension is not automatic and has not been approved at the cutoff. Applicants may need time to gather evidence, so preserving a fair intake window matters independently of a successful launch demonstration.

The public information pages are ordinary static pages. The transactional workflow adds login, eligibility answers, evidence upload, declaration, submission and receipt. A feature switch can keep applications closed while leaving program information and a contact route available. Information-only publishing is not the same as opening intake. Existing account holders can still read saved drafts if no migration occurs. The Trust owns application decisions and applicant communications. LanternPath hosts the application and can propose operational changes but cannot decide eligibility or accept an application on someone's behalf without a recorded instruction.

Imani coordinates procurement and can request reports; she cannot accept an unresolved technical deliverable. Digital service manager Ruth Dene can accept a temporary operational service within Ada's approved launch envelope. Ruth cannot alter the annual fee or certify product conformance. Applicant liaison Dev Shah receives user reports and may arrange an optional test session. His technical observations are evidence, not signatory approval. The Trust's external implementation agency supplies content and has no authority to share live applicant material with LanternPath sales.

The signed order names the core application flow as required for launch and refers to the attached accessibility schedule. A September sales demonstration used a small sample with no evidence upload. The subsequent implementation plan included the new upload-and-declaration module. That distinction is material: confidence in the old demonstration does not establish whether an applicant can finish today's full workflow. The board wants a truthful operational recommendation by 16:30, including what is known, what remains pending and who can decide; it has not demanded a particular recommendation.
# E03 — Applicant liaison complaint and requested response

Record version: TICKET-614.3. Authenticated Trust thread. Original complaint 2026-11-20 14:10 UTC; latest message 2026-11-23 11:35 UTC. Owner: Dev Shah, applicant liaison.

Dev reports that a volunteer tester using keyboard navigation and a screen reader could enter eligibility answers but could not independently complete the evidence-and-declaration stage. Focus moved behind a dialog after an upload error, the error was not announced, and the final declaration control could not reliably be found. Another volunteer using a keyboard without a screen reader became stuck in the evidence picker. Dev says these failures affect a task people must complete to apply; describing them as cosmetic defects would not answer the complaint. The volunteers used synthetic application material and were not applicants seeking preferential treatment.

On November 20 Dev asked for an accessible independent way to submit, the scope of the supplier's prior accessibility claims, a named technical owner and a realistic update before the board pack. He did not ask for medical proof, a legal conclusion or a universal guarantee. The initial response suggested that a family member could help and attached a generic checklist. Dev replied that assistance may expose income and employment evidence, that not everyone has a trusted helper, and that an application route should not require applicants to reveal a disability to obtain ordinary service. That is a practical privacy and dignity concern, not an allegation that every assisted service is necessarily unacceptable.

The latest message confirms the Trust will not collect applicant passwords for staff entry. Dev can explain a voluntary assisted route if it preserves applicant control and is one option among usable choices. He cannot agree that the same failed widget is suitable merely because a support agent can operate it with a mouse. An instructional video would not let the tester tab to an unreachable control. Asking the tester to try a different browser without identifying the known defect would consume time and could imply the report is not credible.

Dev has already provided the browser and screen-reader versions in E08. He will join a short session today at 15:40 with Ruth and one volunteer if invited before 15:15. The volunteer can decline without affecting the complaint. Testing must use fabricated evidence files; a recording requires specific optional permission and must not capture unrelated desktop content. Dev wants a written alternative if no session occurs. Support should not make progress depend on the availability of this particular volunteer, who is not the vendor's unpaid quality team.

The Trust asks that any response distinguish the immediate intake decision from the longer repair and conformance program. It wants to know whether information pages can publish, whether applications can actually open, and whether notice can be corrected before 18:00. The request remains live even if a service credit is later considered. Dev's frustration concerns exclusion, wasted testing time and trust in procurement statements. Neither the complaint nor the polite signoff grants launch consent, a case closure, a release, permission to quote the tester publicly or agreement to a more expensive plan.
# E04 — Signed accessibility schedule and acceptance boundary

Record version: ACC-SCH-2.0. Attached to September 14 order. Signed by Ada Fen and Lena Orr. Effective 2026-09-14. Maintained by LanternPath contracts operations; file annotation updated 2026-11-23 11:30 UTC.

The schedule requires the delivered applicant workflow to be evaluated against WCAG 2.2 Level AA and to permit applicants to complete the agreed core process using supported keyboard and screen-reader combinations. The supplier will provide a dated accessibility assessment identifying scope, method, known exceptions and remediation status. The schedule does not say that an automated scan is certification. It contains no representation that a government body, W3C or a standards organization has certified LanternPath. No separate certification document is in the contract file. An accessibility statement is a communication record and does not replace the agreed assessment.

Acceptance requires a documented walkthrough of the agreed core process, a defect list and Ruth's written acceptance for the Trust. Acceptance may be withheld for a critical blocker. A critical blocker means a confirmed failure preventing an intended applicant from completing a required step without disproportionate or unsafe assistance, where no approved practical alternative is operating. This is a contractual severity definition used by these fictional parties. It is not a claim about statutory thresholds. The schedule permits a temporary alternative by written operational agreement that identifies scope, limitations, owners, review date and treatment of already saved work. Such an agreement does not assert that the primary workflow conforms or erase open defects.

A temporary service may preserve the planned opening date if the relevant launch authority agrees. An operations acceptance can cover a substitute intake process without accepting the defective module as complete. Any waiver of contractual rights, fee change or permanent reduction of requirements needs the two commercial signatories. The distinction was included so that practical service protection would not force a rushed commercial settlement. Ruth may approve operations under E07; she cannot sign a blanket release or accept unknown future defects. Support should explain those boundaries in ordinary language if it proposes a temporary process.

The vendor must give a named owner and a remediation plan when a critical blocker is reproduced. It may describe an engineering target as a target. A completion date becomes a customer commitment only when the engineering owner confirms the delivery, test and release dependencies. A failed test must be communicated and cannot be hidden behind a release label. The customer is expected to provide representative synthetic scenarios and promptly decide proposed operational choices, but it is not responsible for designing the vendor's upload widget or proving a disability.

The schedule allows escalation to a joint review if acceptance or scope is disputed. It does not specify an automatic refund, damages award or cancellation on a first complaint. The main agreement contains ordinary negotiated remedies, none invoked at this cutoff. Contracts operations has not determined whether the August sales correspondence creates additional obligations. The signed schedule remains usable evidence while that question is reviewed; an unresolved legal interpretation is not a reason to withhold a practical incident update or continue a misleading marketing claim.
# E05 — Current release and accessibility incident policy

Record version: REL-5.1. Owner: product operations director Anya Cole. Effective 2026-11-01. Applies to new public transactional launches and critical user barriers.

A reproduced critical barrier in the required production process changes the launch record to blocked pending an authorized disposition. The blocker must identify the affected task, environment, practical user impact and any safe interim service. Blocked does not mean all static pages must be taken offline. Staff should distinguish a product deployment from a customer's public opening: an engineering release does not itself authorize the customer's intake launch. Account executives and support associates cannot override a critical-barrier flag to protect a sales milestone.

A temporary alternative requires a named operations owner, documented end-to-end test evidence, data handling review and customer operational acceptance. The product operations director may approve use within a specific customer and period. The record must state what is substituted, how applicants discover it, what happens if it fails, and when it is reviewed. Customer agreement to a limited temporary service does not certify the primary product or amend commercial terms. Material scope changes, new data destinations, extra populations or a different vendor require the stated reviewers to revisit the approval. Absence of a reply is not customer acceptance.

Support duty leads may immediately stop a scheduled application-opening job when a newly reproduced barrier presents foreseeable harm. The lead must notify the launch owner, preserve information access and record the state. This short protective stop lasts up to forty-eight hours, allowing a signatory decision rather than an indefinite support veto. Extending beyond that period requires product operations confirmation. A duty lead may prepare customer options and coordinate tests but cannot announce final acceptance, publish an invented completion date or withdraw the customer's public notices without its designated owner.

Engineering fixes require regression coverage for successful and unsuccessful submissions, including error recovery, duplicate attempts, upload limits, declaration and receipt. Passing only the originally reported interaction is insufficient for a release recommendation. A provisional test result may support a scoped operational decision; its limitations must travel with it. A scanner result cannot be called a complete assessment. Release notes must identify remaining known barriers, and old claims cannot remain approved simply because an engineering ticket is open.

Public claims of accessibility, certification or conformance must be supported by an assessment with a matching scope and date. On discovery of a material contradictory barrier, the claims owner must contain and correct the claim through the publishing process. Preserve the earlier statement and recipients for a proportionate correction; deleting a webpage alone does not inform a customer who relied on a sales attachment. Legal review handles actual interpretive disputes, while factual limitations can be disclosed by their operational owners. A customer complaint must not be conditioned on purchase, publicity consent or silence. This policy replaces REL-4.2; the older checklist remains archived for explaining prior workflow, not current launch authority.
# E06 — Archived launch checklist and incomplete green status

Record version: REL-4.2/ARCHIVE-19. Owner: delivery operations. Effective 2026-06-01 through 2026-10-31; archived November 1. Historical review compiled 2026-11-23 12:15 UTC. This is historical process evidence, not current approval.

The old checklist let the implementation manager mark an account ready after a content review, smoke test and automated accessibility scan of five representative pages. It required an exception ticket for serious manual findings but did not clearly distinguish static information pages from the complete application flow. A team could obtain a green dashboard with a functioning login and an untested upload dialog. The dashboard's short label was intended for internal scheduling. Some sales staff later pasted it into customer decks as launch readiness, although the checklist did not grant authority to make conformance or certification statements.

Rivermere's October 22 run used this procedure. The five scanned routes were the home page, funding criteria, contact page, login and an empty eligibility page. The new evidence widget did not appear in the scanned state because the test account had no eligible draft. The file record says zero severe automated findings on those routes. It does not say zero accessibility barriers, complete manual testing or acceptance by Ruth. The scan operator did not use a screen reader. The report's export footer omitted those scope limitations, making the later screenshot especially easy to overread.

An October 24 project note from former implementation manager Noel Pike says green means the website is safe for the campaign team to prepare notices. The same note asks for a manual application walkthrough before opening intake. Noel left the project on November 5. A calendar invitation still names him as launch approver, but the November authority table supersedes that delegation. His old note cannot authorize a launch after a new critical finding. The inaccurate calendar entry has not yet been corrected in the coordination system; it helps explain a routing delay, rather than proving that no current owner exists.

An October 29 release rehearsal also has a green badge. It concerns build 8.3 without the November 12 upload change. The developer successfully submitted a sample using a mouse. There is no keyboard-only error-path recording, screen-reader result or rejected-upload retest. A separate table showing high contrast for the campaign logo is accurate within its scope and irrelevant to whether the declaration can be reached. Both records should remain available instead of being silently edited to appear more comprehensive. Their limited scope matters to the correction of the sales attachment.

The current policy requires a new blocked status when a critical barrier is reproduced. Delivery has preserved the old dashboard for audit but has permission to append a visible current-state note. A proposed dashboard automation would expire readiness badges after a module change; it is not deployed. Staff must use the actual authority and current evidence at the cutoff, not a planned automation. There is no factual basis to blame Ruth for failing to understand that a green internal badge concealed an untested step when the customer-facing export never described that limitation.
# E07 — Launch authority and temporary-service approval

Record version: AUTH-7/LA-19. Owner: Anya Cole, product operations director. Authority table effective 2026-11-01. Case approval LA-19 signed 2026-11-23 13:10 UTC; operational execution pending. Case-file annotation by Elise Ward added 2026-11-23 14:40 UTC after E19 arrived; that annotation does not amend the signed approval.

Support duty lead Elise Ward may stop Rivermere's scheduled application-opening job through November 25 at 15:00 under REL-5.1 and preserve information pages. She must verify the job state, notify Ruth and give an update today. She cannot extend the subscription period, issue a £6,000 refund, authorize applicant processing by a new party or declare a repaired product conformant. The product engineering owner is Dan Vale. Anya owns release exceptions. Ruth owns customer operational acceptance; Ada retains the public program decision and commercial signature. Lena owns vendor fee variations. The public launch remains blocked at the cutoff.

LA-19 approves, through November 30 at 17:00, a temporary service using Simple Intake version 2.3 for Rivermere's direct applicants only. Preconditions are Data Steward confirmation of the existing tenant data destination, preservation of saved drafts and their submission status, completion of the failed-submission retest specified in E10, Ruth's written acceptance of the stated limitations, and Ada's recorded agreement to open the program using that scope. Product operations can rely on the recorded test results without waiting for a complete product-wide conformance assessment. The approval is not an instruction to launch regardless of the conditions, and it does not cover a different form version or partner-import batch.

The approved scope permits evidence upload directly to Rivermere's existing protected tenant storage with individual applicant authentication. It includes a published contact route and a no-penalty process for a failed or delayed submission. The Trust must decide any deadline adjustment; no extension is represented as already granted. Operational availability is staffed daily from 08:00 to 18:00, with monitoring outside those hours for service failure but no guaranteed staffed submission assistance overnight. Applicants must see those actual limits. The approval is silent on product fees and cannot be sold as an upgraded package.

If preconditions cannot be evidenced before today's 16:30 customer update, keep transactional opening stopped and information pages available while Anya and Ruth decide the next checkpoint. Anya is available at 16:00 and has reserved a 16:20 escalation call. Those slots do not guarantee an approval outcome. Elise can prepare a deferral notice and test results for the Trust to use; only the Trust can send its program notice. Anya can extend the protective stop after receiving the impact and recovery record. Delaying this launch does not close the complaint or stop work on claims correction.

The 14:40 annotation records that one signed sentence delegates to the customer operations manager authority for 'associated intake administration within the approved population.' In drafting, Anya meant routine notices and duplicate reconciliation. The signed text does not define whether a newly imported partner queue is within that population. The E19 partner record was not attached when LA-19 was signed. Anya has not supplied a subsequent interpretation. Staff proposing material expansion must preserve that ambiguity for the named decision owner, rather than silently treating the broad phrase as unlimited delegation. Nothing here approves shared credentials, private email evidence transfers or undisclosed exclusion of applicants.
# E08 — Reproduced barriers and engineering investigation

Record version: ENG-614.4. Owner: Dan Vale. Last substantive update 2026-11-23 12:10 UTC. Environment: production-equivalent build 8.4, synthetic Rivermere applications, identical feature flags to intended launch.

Dan reproduced the error-path focus failure on Windows 11 with Firefox 144 and NVDA 2025.3 and reproduced an unreachable evidence-picker close control using keyboard navigation in Chrome 142. These are the environments tested, not a claim that the failure occurs only there. After rejecting an oversized file, the modal announces neither the error nor the remaining choices in the tested screen-reader session. Focus returns behind the modal. Repeated tab presses cycle background navigation, and the required declaration cannot be reached through the visible sequence. Refreshing restores the page but discards unsubmitted field edits in the current session.

The defect is in LanternPath's November 12 evidence component, not in the Trust's content. The integration agency cannot repair its keyboard event handling through theme settings. Disabling the evidence step would permit a draft to advance but would remove required evidence without an approved operational collection process. The backend receives no final submission in the reproduced failure, so a visible saved draft is not a received application. Dan has found no corruption of previously completed applications in the small test dataset. That does not prove absence of unrelated issues in every tenant or every browser.

The happy path works for Dan using a mouse with an accepted small file. A developer demonstration with that interaction cannot refute the reported failure. An automated scanner did not exercise the dialog after server-side file rejection; its clean report therefore does not contradict the manual result.
